section_title: Where does David turn when his conscience troubles him?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 10 After David had numbered the troops, his conscience was stricken and he said to the LORD, “I have sinned greatly in what I have done. Now, O LORD, I beg You to take away the iniquity of Your servant, for I have acted very foolishly.” 11 When David got up in the morning, the word of the LORD had come to Gad the prophet, David’s seer: 12 “Go and tell David that this is what the LORD says: ‘I am offering you three options. Choose one of them, and I will carry it out against you.’”

13 So Gad went and said to David, “Do you choose to endure three years of famine in your land, three months of fleeing the pursuit of your enemies, or three days of plague upon your land? Now then, think it over and decide how I should reply to Him who sent me.” 14 David answered Gad, “I am deeply distressed. Please, let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for His mercies are great; but do not let me fall into the hands of men.”

context_lines: After the count, David’s conscience is stricken. He confesses that he has sinned greatly and acted foolishly, and asks the LORD to take away his guilt.

God sends the prophet Gad with three choices: three years of famine, three months fleeing enemies or three days of plague. David is deeply distressed and asks to fall into the LORD’s hand because His mercies are great, rather than into human hands.
Confession does not make the consequences disappear. Yet David’s response turns from insisting on his own decision to depending on God’s mercy.
common_interpretation_lines: [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/2_samuel/24.htm) emphasizes both awakened conscience and trust in mercy. He understands David’s choice as placing him under the same danger as the people, rather than choosing a hardship from which a king might shelter himself.

[Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/24.htm) likewise understands the plague as David’s choice from his words and the event that follows, although David does not expressly name that option. The clearest reason he states is his confidence in the LORD’s great mercy.
god_plan_lines: David’s confession connects with the wider biblical call to acknowledge sin honestly before God. In [1 John 1:8–10](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_john/1.htm), denying sin is self-deception; confession meets God’s faithfulness and forgiveness.

That passage gives Christian readers grounds for coming into the light rather than hiding their wrongdoing. David’s story also reminds us that forgiveness and the removal of every earthly consequence are different things.
The connection is confession and dependence on mercy. Samuel’s account of David receiving three choices does not promise that everyone will be offered a choice of consequences.
